[6] Forecasts indicated that a victory for Donald Trump could cause the peso to weaken to more than 21 per U.S. dollar, a level not seen in over two years. [6] Conversely, a win for Kamala Harris was predicted to strengthen the peso to approximately 18.50 per dollar, although analysts noted that she was also likely to implement relatively protectionist trade policies. [6] <2> The 14th U.S.-Mexico CEO Dialogue took place in Mexico City over two days, from October 14 to October 15, 2024. The event brought together Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, members of her cabinet, and over 200 business leaders from both the United States and Mexico. This was President Sheinbaum's first significant meeting with U.S. business leaders since her inauguration. Organized by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and Mexico's Consejo Coordinador Empresarial (CCE), the dialogue focused on enhancing the bilateral economic relationship, with discussions centered on the USMCA trade agreement, fostering private investment, trade facilitation, and energy policy. During the event, President Sheinbaum's administration announced investment commitments of over $20 billion from various international companies. <3> The Conference Board reported a significant drop in U.S. consumer confidence in September 2024, with the index falling to 98.7 from an upwardly revised 105.6 in August. This marked the largest one-month decline since August 2021. The deterioration in consumer sentiment was attributed to growing concerns about the labor market and a more pessimistic outlook on future business conditions and income. Specifically, consumers' assessments of current business and labor market conditions worsened, as did their expectations for the short term. The decline was most pronounced among consumers aged 35 to 54 and those earning less than $50,000. Despite the drop in confidence, the Expectations Index remained above the threshold that typically signals an impending recession. <4> On August 5, 2024, the Institute for Supply Management (ISM) reported that its Services Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) registered 51.4% in July 2024, an increase of 2.6 percentage points from the June reading of 48.8%. [1, 3] This figure surpassed market expectations of a rise to 51.0. The return to expansion territory indicated growth in the U.S. services sector for the 47th time in the last 50 months. [1, 3] The growth was driven by key sub-indexes returning to expansion, with the Business Activity Index registering 54.5%, the New Orders Index at 52.4%, and the Employment Index rising to 51.1%. [2, 3] Ten industries within the services sector reported growth during the month of July. [1] <5> On August 2, 2024, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics released its jobs report for July 2024, which showed a significant slowdown in the labor market. [12] The economy added 114,000 jobs, falling well short of economists' consensus forecast of 175,000. [1, 2] Concurrently, the unemployment rate rose from 4.1% in June to 4.3%, its highest level since October 2021. [1] This weaker-than-expected data intensified concerns about a potential economic slowdown. As a result, the report led to increased expectations among investors and analysts that the Federal Reserve would be more likely to implement an interest rate cut in September. [1] However, some viewpoints suggested that the risk of a recession remained low, viewing the rising unemployment as a potentially healthy sign of more people entering the workforce. [4] <6> The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) concluded its two-day meeting on July 31, 2024, and decided to maintain the federal funds rate at a target range of 5.25% to 5.50%, a level it has held for over a year. [2] The committee's accompanying statement was viewed by some as a \"hawkish\" hold, signaling that imminent rate cuts were not forthcoming. The statement noted that while there has been \"some further progress\" toward the 2% inflation objective, inflation remains somewhat elevated. [2] In a press conference following the meeting, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell acknowledged the significant decline in inflation and recognized that there are now real downside risks to the employment mandate. [1, 3] Powell's comments and a change in the FOMC's statement, which shifted from being \"highly attentive to inflation risks\" to being \"attentive to the risks to both sides of its dual mandate,\" suggested a potential rate cut could be considered as early as the September meeting, contingent on incoming economic data. The stronger-than-expected economic performance, driven by robust consumer spending and business investment, defied expectations of a slowdown. [2, 3] This 12-month increase was smaller than the 3.3 percent increase for the year ending in May. [2, 3] The index for all items less food and energy, a closely watched measure of core inflation, rose 3.3 percent over the last 12 months, which was the smallest 12-month increase for that index since April 2021. [3, 4] <9> The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the U.S. economy added 206,000 nonfarm payroll jobs in June 2024. [1, 2, 3, 12] Job growth in June was concentrated in the government, health care, social assistance, and construction sectors. [2, 3] Average hourly wage growth showed signs of cooling, with the year-over-year increase at its lowest rate in the post-pandemic period. [2, 8] Participants observed that labor demand and supply were coming into better balance and that the economy was growing at a solid pace.
